title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). The experiment used a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine). A single shared initial candidate was generated per task by gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120). A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks and triggered ≤1 repair only when validator.violation_count>0. Outcomes: baseline success = 120/120 (1.00); guarded success = 120/120 (1.00). Contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Validator traces show repair_applied=false for all guarded episodes. We incorporate peer-review clarifications (shared-generation semantics, repair-trigger logic, and artifact-grounded explanation of statistical degeneracy), expand methodology and execution accounting, and provide reproducibility guidance grounded in archived artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can produce human-readable network configuration commands from natural-language intent, promising faster NetOps workflows. However, plausible-looking commands may nonetheless violate workflow constraints (for example, requiring a shutdown step before changing MTU or making unsafe uplink switchover sequences), produce regressions, or break invariants that a live network depends on. Prior proposals therefore recommend integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers into LLM-driven NetOps pipelines so that generated candidates are checked and, when necessary, repaired before enactment. Evaluating such guarded pipelines requires closed-loop executable tests that expose semantic/network-level failures beyond token- or syntax-level correctness.

We studied whether adding an executable emulator validator and a single-step repair mechanism reduces emulator-observed semantic failures relative to an LLM-only suggestion workflow under a tightly scoped, preregistered paired design. Our confirmatory research question (preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) asked: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair effects from generation variance we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: the same generation was presented to both conditions for each task. This isolates the marginal effect of validation/repair on identical generator outputs. The present paper reports the preregistered design, exact execution accounting, confirmatory statistical results, per-topology counts, representative validator traces, and an artifact-grounded interpretation of a degenerate ceiling outcome observed in the run.
sections.related_work:
Prior work emphasizes that evaluating generated configuration text alone misses operational failure modes caused by ordering, transient constraints, or inter-dependent fields. Recent executable benchmarks and testbeds (for example, NetConfArena and related efforts) evaluate agentic behavior inside emulators or digital twins so closed-loop consequences are observable. Other studies report iterative generate→validate→repair architectures and tool-augmented agents to detect and correct semantic errors before enactment. Surveys of agentic NetOps and AIOps document proposed guardrails such as canaries, veto layers, translation-to-formal-model patterns, and constrained repair budgets.

Where many prior studies compare end-to-end systems across models and tool stacks, our experiment takes a complementary, narrowly scoped approach: it holds the generator fixed and asks whether the validator/repair stage provides incremental safety benefits for identical generated candidates. This isolates an important mechanism often conflated with generator variance in multi-component studies. The literature gaps motivating our work include scarce production-rooted incident corpora, limited cross-model comparisons under identical executable harnesses, and under-explored calibrated uncertainty estimates for structured configuration outputs. Those gaps informed our preregistered emphasis on deterministic archival and detailed execution accounting so future cross-run comparisons can reuse the same task bank, validator, and manifests.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and experimental logic: The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) and archived before execution. The preregistration defined a paired-binary design with exactly N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks, deterministically assigned into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine) with 40 tasks each. Each task produced a single shared initial candidate generated by gpt-5-mini; that shared candidate was supplied unchanged to both conditions (baseline, guarded) to isolate the validator/repair marginal effect. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed by the exact two-sided McNemar test; complementary reporting included a bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). The preregistration mandated that a guarded repair be applied only when the emulator validator reported validator.violation_count>0 and that at most one repair iteration be used per guarded episode.

Generation, prompting, and model configuration: All shared initial candidates were produced by the declared hosted model (gpt-5-mini) and recorded in execution/responses/*. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 120 and stage accounting shows shared_initial_generation = 120. The archived execution/model_configuration.json contains the declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini and provider = openai_responses; the run used one generation call per task (maximum_attempts_per_call = 1). The paired design parameter independent_condition_generation=false (preregistered) enforces identical generator outputs per pair so that any difference in outcomes arises from the subsequent validation/repair logic.

Task bank, constraints, and validator semantics: The task corpus is a deterministic synthetic set produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest entry encodes: initial_state, expected_final_state, an explicit required_sequence of field changes (for example, shut→mtu→vlan→restore), workflow_policies (for example, must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints), and a difficulty label (medium/hard/very_hard) with dependency_rule_count and required_command_count. The guarded pipeline integrated a deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, validator_version = 5.0) that executed full_intent_constraint_validation checks and produced structured validator_trace artifacts containing validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. The preregistered repair policy invoked a single repair only when violation_count>0; repair prompts and repair_provider_trace artifacts would be archived if used.

Instrumentation, contamination controls, and accounting: The execution harness enforced deterministic emulator-state resets between tasks and recorded provider-call audits. The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact confirms provider_call_audit counts (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cache_miss_count = 120). Contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection, cross-condition cache-key reuse) were applied and logged; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty. The preregistration specified exclusion rules for technical/instrumentation failures; analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports zero exclusions and complete_pairs = 120. All raw provider traces, responses, scorer JSONs, and analysis artifacts were archived for reproducibility.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and main outcomes: The run completed the planned episodes (planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240) and produced one shared initial generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline = 120 successes, 0 failures and guarded = 120 successes, 0 failures (success rates = 1.0 for both conditions). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Missingness and contamination artifacts indicate no technical exclusions and no flagged contamination.

Confirmatory statistics and interpretation: With zero discordant pairs the exact two-sided McNemar p-value equals 1.0. The paired-difference point estimate is 0.00. The preregistered bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) equals [0.00, 0.00]; this degenerate CI is an artifact-grounded statistical consequence of resampling an empirical paired table with no discordant observations: every bootstrap resample reproduces the same concordant-success counts, yielding zero-width intervals. The analysis/analysis_log.jsonl records these bootstrap parameters and the completed paired analysis event.

Per-topology breakdown and representative diagnostics: Tasks were deterministically assigned 40 per topology class. Aggregated counts from archived artifacts are:
- Edge (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Core (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Leaf–spine (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
Representative scoring JSONs (for example, execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json and -baseline.json) show normalized_response equal to normalized_reference_answer, parsed_command_count equal to required_command_count, validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, and validator_trace.repair_applied = false. The exemplar traces demonstrate the validator's structured fields (validation_before/after, touched_field counts, violation lists), enabling independent reconstruction of validator logic.

Repair activity and secondary endpoints: The guarded repair policy would apply a single repair when validator.violation_count>0. Because violation_count = 0 for every guarded episode, repair_applied = false across the archive and no repair_provider_trace artifacts exist. Consequently, preregistered secondary endpoints (proportion of tasks requiring repair, mean repair calls per task) are vacuous for this run. Analysis artifacts documenting these null repair outcomes are present under execution/scoring/ and analysis/.

Deterministic reconciliation and audit: analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms consistent episode accounting and provider-call audits. The execution manifest records run start and completion timestamps (started_at_utc = 2026-08-29T00:39:14.248966+00:00; completed_at_utc = 2026-08-29T00:48:37.619198+00:00). analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty. These artifacts collectively demonstrate that the observed ceiling outcome is not attributable to missingness, contamination, or instrumentation failure.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling/null outcome: The shared-generation paired design intentionally removed generation variance so that any difference between conditions would arise solely from the validator/repair stage operating on identical candidates. In this experiment the shared initial candidates produced by gpt-5-mini all satisfied the deterministic emulator validator's encoded intent constraints and workflow policies, producing a concordant-success ceiling (n_11=120). Under these conditions the guarded pipeline could not exercise repair behavior and therefore could not reduce semantic failures relative to baseline. The observed exact McNemar p=1.0 and bootstrap CI=[0.00,0.00] are statistical manifestations of this ceiling.

Methodological implications and recommendations: The paired shared-generation design answers a precise mechanistic question — whether a validator/repair stage can improve outcomes for identical generator outputs — and the answer in this task bank and under the archived generator/prompting configuration is "no effect" because the generator produced only valid candidates. This narrow null result should not be extrapolated to imply that guarded pipelines are unnecessary in broader settings. To evaluate practical repair utility we recommend confirmatory tests that allow independent per-condition generation so guards can act on generator errors. Additional recommendations (all consistent with archived artifacts and feasible under the same harness) include: (1) expanding the repair budget to permit multiple repair iterations; (2) testing multiple generator models and prompt perturbation schemes; (3) introducing adversarial/noisy task variants; and (4) incorporating multi-vendor behavioral models into the validator.

Threats to validity: Construct validity — the deterministic emulator validator operationalizes semantic correctness via encoded workflow policies (must_be_down_for_fields, make-before-break patterns) present in each task payload; while reproducible, this deterministic logic simplifies real production heterogeneity. Internal validity — the paired design removes generation variance (intended) but thereby precludes observing guard effects that depend on generator errors. External validity — the synthetic deterministic task corpus abstracts away vendor heterogeneity and partial observability found in live networks; therefore generalization to production deployments is limited. Conclusion validity — the preregistered power assumptions targeted an absolute reduction of 0.15 in semantic-failure rate; because the baseline succeeded on the entire curated task set the primary test could not detect the targeted effect and is therefore uninformative for that hypothesized magnitude.

Operational implications: Even when the validator was unused in this run, the archived validator traces provide valuable operator-facing artifacts: per-episode validation_before/after summaries, explicit lists of violation codes (empty in this run), touched-field counts, and normalized configuration representations. These structured traces permit explainability, post-hoc audits, and forensics in the event of production incidents. The provider-call audit and deterministic reconciliation artifacts show how to instrument LLM-driven NetOps runs for accountable operation and can support operator trust and governance frameworks.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing n_11=120 (baseline and guarded successes) and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed=1729). The result documents a ceiling effect on this curated synthetic task bank and clarifies that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we demonstrate how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and we show how deterministic archival artifacts (responses, scoring JSONs, analysis/ artifacts, and provider-call audits) support reproducible failure analyses and informed design recommendations for future experiments.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
